title: Multi-instrumentalists Ade Monsbourgh and Warwick Dyer
summary: Monsbourgh plays every instrument, now tenor in a Hawkins ballad style; Dyer doubled piano as a tuneful drum and was a hot trombonist.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: eight Monsborough is a classic example. Yes. It is really exceptional. It's just that he appears on so many records, I think, that might give you that impression. There isn't really very much doubling, except when eight does it. What all has he played since you've known him? What instruments? Oh, well, every instrument. Every instrument. He's quit the alto. He's changed to tenor. And plays that very well, as he plays most instruments. He was first known as Plunk Monsborough. He used to play banjo. As I say, he's played all instruments. And what kind of tenor does he play now? What style? It reminds me of, say, mid-thirties, Coleman Hawkins breathing through ballads sort of thing. Very nice, subtle sort of stuff. Most Australian stuff is a bit, I suppose, not very, not very deep. And, Aid is an exception. He's, he's a more subtle player. Most of us just aren't, probably, good enough to, to do much more than, blow out a fairly loud noise.
We didn't really get on with Warwick Dyer. He, he doubles him. Do you play piano?

Yes, um, a sort of limited but very, um, knocked out piano. Yes. Um, he was good to play with, uh, when he was playing piano because he, uh, he, uh, definitely regarded the piano as a, a tuneful drum. And, uh, beat out the chords, uh, strongly, which was great. He was, um, he was a very, um, very good, uh, trombone player, a very, uh, very hot trombone player.
